It adapts its execution path based on the number of intersection candidates (workload) for the rays in the warp [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the algorithm checks if all rays in a warp have intersection candidates. If not, it checks for rays with 'high workload' (defined as at least 16 intersection candidates). Based on the number of such rays (specifically, if there are more than 20), the execution path proceeds with the standard intersection routine. Otherwise, it uses a shared memory buffer to process high-workload rays in pairs. This confirms that the execution path adapts based on the number of intersection candidates (workload).
supported

The claim states that SIMD efficiency is tied to ray coherence. Both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly state: 'This is the case because we parallelize by assigning different rays to each thread, which ties SIMD efficiency to ray coherence.' Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim.

# [S2, unofficial] Atomic increment on a shared counter to get unique position

The claim states that the evidence supports the use of an atomic increment on a shared counter to get a unique position for inserting high-workload rays into a shared memory buffer. The source text explicitly confirms this: 'If we have determined that standard packetization would be inefficient and there are rays with high workload, we insert those into a buffer in shared memory. This is done with an atomic increment on a shared counter.' The text further explains that this allows storing the ray index and first intersection candidate, which aligns with the claim's context of distributing work for single rays to many threads to improve SIMD utilization.

It sets itself apart from standard packetization by distributing the work of a single ray across multiple threads when the number of intersection candidates is high, thereby maintaining throughput even when rays traverse cells with varying densities [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

This confirms that the work distribution is triggered by high workload (many candidates) and is intended to improve efficiency (throughput/SIMD utilization).
